conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Patel. You were brought in after a fall. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah… I had a lot to drink last night—like a pint and a half of vodka. I got dizzy and just fell forward. Hit my face on the ground.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Did you lose consciousness at any point?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I was awake the whole time. Just felt really shaky and weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ve done some tests. Your CT scan of the head is normal—no bleeding or fracture. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks… I was worried about that. My head hurts a little, but mostly my chest and shoulder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you mentioned chest pain. How long has that been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: About four days. It’s in the middle, behind my breastbone. Feels worse when I move or breathe deep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your EKG and blood tests—no signs of a heart attack. The pain is likely from the fall, maybe bruised muscles.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I was scared it was my heart again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Actually, your heart rate was very fast when you arrived—around 130 to 140. And it’s irregular. You’re in atrial fibrillation again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Again? I had that last time. But I stopped taking the medicine… it made me tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but not taking it puts you at risk for stroke or heart failure. We gave you some medication in the ER to slow your heart rate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I remember the IV. But my heart’s still racing a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started you on a new medication called diltiazem. It’s working better than the last one. Your rate is coming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that the one I take once a day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, an extended-release version. You’ll take one pill daily at the same time. It’s very important you don’t miss doses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. But sometimes I forget, or I don’t have the meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s hard. But this time, we’re sending the prescription to a care pharmacy you can access. No cost.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That helps. Thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning again. I’m checking in. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. My heart feels slower. Still a little sore in the chest and shoulder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an X-ray of your shoulder—no fracture. The pain is likely from the fall. We’ll keep managing it with mild painkillers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the chest X-ray? Anything there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your lungs look clear. There’s mild heart enlargement, but that’s been stable. Nothing urgent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your lab results are back. Your liver enzymes are a bit high, which can happen with heavy drinking, but nothing dangerous right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know I drink too much. But I don’t feel sick from it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not about feeling sick. Alcohol can trigger atrial fibrillation and make it harder to control. It also affects your liver and brain over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I should cut back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Ideally, stop completely. But if not, at least reduce. We’re giving you thiamine, folic acid, and a multivitamin to help protect your body.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take them. The banana bag they gave me earlier helped with the nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Heart rate is in the 90s, regular. We’re going to keep monitoring you tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I might go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if things stay stable. We want to make sure your heart stays under control and you’re safe to leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news. Your labs this morning look better. Hemoglobin is up, liver enzymes improving. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do when I get out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your diltiazem every day at the same time. Also take the thiamine, folic acid, and multivitamin. Avoid alcohol as much as possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if my heart starts racing again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Go to the ER immediately. Also, follow up with the homeless health clinic next week. They’ll help you stay on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for not giving up on me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself. We’re here to help.
